A new actual tunneling time formulation is proposed, which is based on the idea that tunneling time is equivalent to a specific type of clock's slowdown within the tunneling barrier. This formulation is then compared to previous theories, including the H\"{a}gg formulation, and it is shown that it is consistent with spin fluctuations caused by a clock's slowdown within the tunneling barrier. Furthermore, it is proposed that the formulation can be used to explain the Gamow energy shift, and it is shown that the new formulation is consistent with the energy-time uncertainty principle.

This study examines the influence of relativistic adjustments on amplitudes 
featuring P-wave charmonia mesons, with the expectation that these corrections 
will be substantial. We utilize a light-cone QCD sum rule to determine the 
impact of relativistic corrections on the form factors of the $B_c \to B^{(*)}$ 
processes involving P-wave charmonia mesons. Our findings indicate that 
relativistic corrections can reach up to 20% in these form factors.

We have developed a theoretical framework for implementing interferometry using nonlinear Hadamard gates within a Bose-Einstein condensate. Our findings indicate that a specific type of nonlinear interaction can be used to create these gates, which can then be applied to a Bose-Einstein condensate to achieve a specific type of interferometry. Our research shows that a specific type of interferometry can be achieved with a specific type of nonlinearity, which can then be used to measure the properties of a Bose-Einstein condensate. Our findings also indicate that a specific type of interferometry can be achieved with a specific type of nonlinearity, which can then be used to measure the properties of a Bose-Einstein condensate. Our research has significant implications for the study of quantum systems and the development of new technologies.

We examine the properties of the $eBMS$ charges in the context of the Kerr black
hole, with a focus on the near horizon regime. The analysis is carried out in the
frame of the Kerr metric, with a specific emphasis on the properties of the
Goldstone modes. The study reveals that the degeneracies of the vacua are linked
to the notions of soft news and Schwarzian modes, with implications for the
entropy of the Kerr black hole. The analysis also shows that the $eBMS$ charges
are invariant under the action of the Kerr metric, with a specific dependence on
the angular momentum of the black hole.

Deep neural networks have become a standard approach in solving various problems, particularly in the field of image classification. However, achieving reliable results often requires extensive training and testing, which can be time-consuming and resource-intensive. To address this issue, we have developed an innovative ensemble method that leverages multiple deep neural networks to enhance classification accuracy. Our proposed method is applied to a real-world dataset, the CIFAR-10, and demonstrates significant improvements in accuracy and reliability. By combining the outputs of multiple networks, our ensemble method outperforms traditional approaches, achieving higher accuracy and more reliable predictions.

This study explores the connections between generalized connections and Ricci-flat metrics, as well as its implications for string theory. We also investigate how these concepts can be used to construct new solutions, as exemplified by the generation of novel heterotic supergravity backgrounds from generalized connections.

This paper provides evidence and specific examples to demonstrate that there are infinitely many irreducible polynomial functions over certain power series and power matrices, resulting in complete mappings for prime powers in the case of the prime's characteristic.

The identification of intestinal parasites is crucial for effective treatment and disease prevention. Although human experts can diagnose parasites, they are prone to errors due to fatigue and inexperience. In contrast, deep learning models have shown promising results in the field of medical image analysis. This study presents a deep learning-based approach for the detection of intestinal parasites in clinical images, utilizing a dataset of 10,000 images collected from 10 countries. Our model, built upon a ResNet architecture, achieved an impressive 89.5% accuracy in parasite detection and 85.1% accuracy in parasite classification.

This paper examines a non-linear integro-differential Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equation system that arises from a non-zero-sum stochastic differential game with Poisson jumps. Under specific conditions, we establish the existence and uniqueness of a viscosity solution to this equation, proving its convergence as well. Our analysis yields a new viscosity solution to the Isaacs equation, and we demonstrate the value function of the stochastic game as its corresponding viscosity solution.

This research introduces a novel control strategy, the Genetic Filter (GF), for controlling a quadcopter in the presence of disturbances. The GF combines a Genetic Algorithm (GA) and a Kalman Filter (KF) to optimize performance. The GA adjusts the KF's parameters to minimize the estimation error covariance, thus improving the estimation accuracy. The proposed control strategy was tested through simulations, where it demonstrated superior performance compared to the Kalman Filter alone, particularly in the presence of disturbances.

The pion-nucleon sigma term is a crucial parameter in understanding nuclear physics, and its relevance has grown significantly in recent years. A new approach to calculating this term is presented, which involves a direct determination from lattice QCD simulations. This method bypasses the need to calculate quark scalar form factors, and instead relies on the finite volume behavior of the correlation functions. A key aspect of this approach is the use of a specific combination of correlation functions, which can be used to extract the sigma term from the exponential decay of the correlation functions in the large time limit. A specific combination of correlation functions is used to cancel out the contributions from excited states, and this method has been tested using data from lattice QCD simulations. A preliminary result for the sigma term is presented, which is consistent with previous calculations, and this method has the potential to provide more precise values in the future.

The CMS silicon pixel detector underwent significant enhancements, including the installation of a new high-performance layer near the beam pipe, which improved its capabilities beyond 2016. This upgrade led to better performance metrics, particularly in tracking low transverse momentum particles. To accommodate higher luminosity levels at the high Luminosity LHC, further enhancements are planned for the 2030s, focusing on increasing the detector's track acceptance and luminosity capabilities. This paper outlines the latest developments in the CMS pixel detector upgrades, including its performance in 2018 and future plans.

We have developed a novel, efficient method for classifying active galactic nuclei (AGN) host galaxies using a deep learning approach. Our approach leverages a pre-trained convolutional neural network (CNN) originally designed for image classification, which is then fine-tuned on a dataset of 100,000 spectroscopically classified AGN host galaxies from the SDSS-IV MaNGA survey. Our model achieves a high level of accuracy, with a 90.5% precision rate for galaxies at redshifts less than 0.2, 80.0% for those between 0.2 and 0.4, and 70.0% for galaxies at redshifts greater than 0.4. Our model's performance is comparable to that of a state-of-the-art machine learning approach, but with significantly reduced computational requirements. Our approach can be easily applied to large-scale imaging surveys, such as the SDSS-IV MaNGA survey, to accurately classify AGN host galaxies.

The influence of nuclear short-range correlations on the thickness of the neutron skin in heavy, asymmetric nuclei is examined. A comparison is made between a model that accounts for these correlations and a traditional model based on the Fermi gas distribution. The analysis reveals that nuclear short-range correlations contribute significantly to neutron skin thickness, with an effect comparable to that of the difference in the nuclear mean-field potentials of neutrons and protons.

The core-collapse supernova progenitor mass range of 8-25 solar masses is a crucial factor in determining the chemical enrichment of the early galaxy. However, the mass distribution of these progenitors remains uncertain, which hinders our understanding of the chemical evolution of the galaxy. To address this issue, we developed a novel method that uses the abundances of iron and nickel in early stars to infer the characteristics of the core-collapse supernova mass distribution. By applying this technique to the data from the Gaia-Enceladus dwarf galaxy, we found that the core-collapse supernova mass distribution is consistent with a uniform distribution from 8 to 25 solar masses. This finding is in line with the predictions of the delayed detonation model, which is a widely accepted model for core-collapse supernovae. Our study demonstrates that the chemical abundances of stars in the Gaia-Enceladus dwarf galaxy can be used to constrain the core-collapse supernova mass distribution, which is a crucial factor in the chemical evolution of the galaxy.

However, the optimization of these models often becomes increasingly difficult as the number of parameters grows, particularly when using the quantum output probability. This study investigates the scalability of the optimization process for both quantum output probability and machine learning regression tasks. The results show that the choice of output significantly impacts the convergence rate of the optimization, with the former being more challenging to optimize. Furthermore, the research demonstrates that the optimization landscape is influenced by the quantum circuit depth, with the former being more sensitive to changes in the circuit depth. The study also reveals that the optimization process is more efficient when the quantum circuit is designed to have a specific structure, with the former being more sensitive to changes in the circuit structure.

This paper focuses on investigating pointwise semi-slant submanifolds within the context of Sasakian manifolds. We establish that pointwise semi-slant submanifolds in Sasakian manifolds can be either warped products or non-decomposable, and we derive the necessary and sufficient conditions for a pointwise semi-slant warped product to exist.

Researchers have successfully conducted an experiment to detect the coherent elastic scattering of neutrinos on a nucleus using a 100-gram, 10-centimeter-diameter germanium crystal. This massive detector, which is highly sensitive to ionization, was cooled to 1.5 Kelvin and placed in a low-radiation environment. A 10-megawatt spallation neutron source was used to generate an intense flux of neutrinos, which were produced as a byproduct of a 100-millisecond pulse lasting 1.5 seconds. A 100-millisecond window was used to analyze the data, which revealed a 99% confidence level that the germanium crystal detected the neutrino interaction. This breakthrough was made possible by the combination of a large detector mass and a highly sensitive ionization detection system.

Active systems, such as cells and micro-swimmers, exhibit motion that can be influenced by their environment. To study this phenomenon, we have developed a model for a pair of rotating particles driven by an external force. The model shows that the particles' motion can be controlled by adjusting their rotation speed, similar to how a steering wheel operates. The results indicate that the particles' motion is affected by their size and the strength of their interaction, and that they can be used to study how external forces affect their behavior.

This study investigates the influence of biased estimators on the temperature maps of the cosmic microwave background (CMB) in the presence of strong point sources. We developed a straightforward model to simulate the effects of biased estimators on CMB maps, which are influenced by strong point sources. Our simulations reveal that the error distribution in these maps is not uniform, but rather is concentrated around the sources, with the error increasing with the sources' flux. Furthermore, our results indicate that the bias in the CMB maps is not solely determined by the sources' flux, but also by the angular distance between the sources and the CMB fluctuations. Our findings have significant implications for the analysis of CMB maps, as they suggest that the bias in these maps can be substantial and must be taken into account in the analysis.

This study introduces a novel framework for instructing large language models on tasks, drawing inspiration from two key ideas: pedagogy and pragmatism. Pedagogy involves guiding the model to learn from its own mistakes, while pragmatism focuses on obtaining satisfactory results with limited resources. Our framework, called PRL, utilizes a teacher-student paradigm where the model is trained to learn from its own mistakes, and employs a teacher to correct its mistakes. We demonstrate the effectiveness of PRL on various natural language generation tasks, including summarization, dialogue generation, and question generation, and show that it outperforms existing methods in terms of both performance and efficiency.

Quantum state tomography is a time-consuming process requiring numerous measurements to accurately reconstruct quantum states. A new technique called shadow tomography can efficiently determine specific properties of quantum states without needing to fully reconstruct them. This method involves creating an ensemble of quantum states and measuring their Pauli correlations, which can then be used to calculate any observable quantity related to the system. A recent study proposed an alternative approach to shadow tomography that can efficiently determine multi-qubit Pauli operators by utilizing the inherent symmetries of these operators. This method has been experimentally validated using a 2-qubit superconducting circuit and has shown significant improvements in measurement efficiency compared to previous techniques.

This study explores how the inradius and circumradius of a two-dimensional convex shape change in response to a given direction. Key findings include the establishment of optimal constant factors for specific inequalities and a demonstration that these factors are the most possible. Additionally, a related inequality is discovered and proven for a volume-related measurement in higher-dimensional convex shapes.

This research paper examines the trajectory design of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) to optimize the time it takes to serve a maximum number of ground users within a specific time frame. The problem is analogous to the development of efficient flight paths for drones, which must balance the need to visit multiple locations with the constraints of battery life and fuel capacity. The proposed solution involves modeling the UAV's movement as a series of discrete time steps, where the UAV can visit multiple users within a specific time frame. The objective is to maximize the number of users served within a specific time frame, subject to constraints such as battery life, fuel capacity, and maximum speed. The proposed solution is shown to be effective in reducing the time it takes to serve a maximum number of users within a specific time frame, and can be applied to a variety of scenarios, including emergency response and delivery services.

Our research shows that the way the molecule is arranged affects its magnetic and electric properties. We found that the molecule's orientation can be influenced by the type of substrate it's placed on, and that this effect can be further manipulated by adjusting the molecule's internal structure. The rapid expansion of the Internet of Things has led to significant concerns about data security and privacy, prompting the need for novel approaches to protect sensitive information. To address these concerns, we propose a new privacy-preserving framework that leverages blockchain technology to provide users with control over their data and the ability to verify the authenticity of IoT devices. This framework enables users to manage access to their data through private keys and issue smart contracts that allow authorized users to retrieve data from authorized IoT devices. To ensure the integrity of the system, we introduce a consensus mechanism that enables users to confirm the legitimacy of IoT devices and flag any unauthorized access attempts. Our proposed solution is evaluated using a testbed, which demonstrates its effectiveness in providing users with enhanced data privacy and security.

This study examines the properties of matrix polynomial bundles, specifically their openness and closedness in relation to their spectral data. We demonstrate that such bundles possess an open nature with respect to their linearization's spectral information, and also address the openness of their finite eigenvalue multiplicities. Furthermore, this research investigates the spectral properties of matrix polynomials within a bundle, focusing on the behavior of their infinite and zero eigenvalues.

A mathematical framework for string theory's generalized geometry is established, where it is shown that a space with a continuous string algebra can be T-dualized if and only if its classical counterpart possesses this property. This insight is further demonstrated by a concrete example of a non-geometric string algebra that fails to be described by a Riemannian or generalized complex structure, thus confirming that these mathematical constructs are not universally applicable to string dualities.

A novel method for graph minor embedding is proposed, enabling efficient transformation between sparser and denser graph classes. This results in significant improvements in algorithm performance for several problems, including solving metric Baker's problems in graph minors more efficiently. The proposed technique allows for a logarithmic factor reduction in running time for problems such as metric TSP and Steiner Tree in graph minors, and more substantial gains for problems such as metric k-Median and k-Center, and Euclidean metric TSP.

This research investigates the asymptotic behavior of solutions to a time-periodic diffusion process, where the rate of convergence is influenced by the frequency of the forcing function. Specifically, we demonstrate that the rate of convergence is directly proportional to the frequency of the forcing function, and that the initial state of the system has a greater impact on the rate of convergence when the frequency is low.

We introduce the Qubit-ADAPT-VQE (QEB-ADAPT-VQE) algorithm, a novel approach that combines the efficiency of the qubit-based ADAPT-VQE with the fast convergence of its fermionic counterpart. By leveraging the inherent limitations of QEB-ADAPT-VQE, we develop a strategy to iteratively refine the Hamiltonian's excitation operator ordering, thereby achieving a balance between efficiency and fast convergence. Our study demonstrates the efficacy of QEB-ADAPT-VQE in reducing computational costs for complex molecules, such as the nitrogen molecule, and shows that it can be effectively implemented on near-term quantum devices.

This paper presents the Deep Generative Decoder (DGD), a novel approach for unsupervised domain adaptation that leverages a pre-trained supervised model. DGD constructs a shared latent space for both source and target domains, where it trains a generative model to map target domain samples to the pre-trained model's input space. By enforcing a generative adversarial network (GAN) loss, DGD ensures that mapped target domain samples are indistinguishable from source domain samples, effectively classifying them in a separate representation. This approach is demonstrated on a range of unsupervised domain adaptation tasks, including image classification and semantic segmentation, and achieves state-of-the-art results on several benchmark datasets.

This study presents an unsupervised voice conversion approach that utilizes a single, pre-trained vocoder and no annotated data. The approach is evaluated using a dataset of over 100 hours of speech and demonstrates its effectiveness through a listening test. The results show that the unsupervised system's speech synthesis quality is comparable to that of a supervised system, with a slight preference for the supervised system in terms of naturalness and intelligibility. The unsupervised system's performance is also found to be sensitive to the amount of training data, with a notable improvement observed when the dataset exceeds 100 hours.

This study examines the interplay between the Tsallis holographic dark energy model's interacting coupling parameter $C_{I}$ and its constant parameter $p$. The research reveals that $C_{I}$ is directly linked to $p$, and the density parameter $\Omega_{DE}$ is influenced by $p$. The analysis shows that the Tsallis model can be considered a specific instance of the more general Interacting Dark Energy (IDE) model. The investigation also investigates the stability of the Tsallis model's constant parameter $p$ and its implications for the model's stability.

In real-world applications, solving complex optimization problems often involves a trade-off between solution quality and computational resources. To address this, we propose the Investment Ratio (IR) metric, which measures the cost of a solution in terms of the additional resources required to achieve the optimal outcome. This metric is particularly useful for evaluating and comparing heuristic solutions, as it provides a clear indication of the potential benefits of seeking an exact solution. We demonstrate the effectiveness of IR through a case study on the k-median problem, where we show that it can be used to guide decision-making and assess the value of exact solutions.
This paper explores the concept of source path and source simply connected groupoid within the framework of synthetic differential geometry, and compares it to the approaches of Raussen and Jess.

This paper introduces Dynaswap, a Web3-powered platform that facilitates the trading of digital assets and workflows. The project prioritizes security through the integration of cutting-edge technologies such as Zero Knowledge Proofs, Multi-Party Computation, and advanced cryptographic algorithms. Dynaswap offers a unique peer-to-peer trading experience, allowing users to exchange assets and workflows without revealing sensitive information. The platform's architecture is designed to support a variety of use cases, including asset trading, workflow trading, and multi-party collaboration. Dynaswap's architecture is built on a decentralized blockchain network, ensuring the integrity and immutability of all transactions. The project's roadmap includes plans for further development and expansion, with a focus on enhancing the user experience and expanding the platform's capabilities.

This research introduces a Supervised Contrastive Pre-training method for Contrastive Sentiment Review Analysis, utilizing annotated review data to enhance sentiment feature extraction. The method employs a Siamese network architecture, consisting of a shared transformer encoder and two distinct contrastive heads, to simultaneously contrast positive and negative sentiment reviews. The approach incorporates a combination of supervised and unsupervised contrastive learning losses, allowing the model to capture both labeled and unlabeled review sentiment information. The proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on three public datasets, demonstrating improved accuracy in sentiment feature extraction and review classification.

A mathematical model has been developed to investigate the link between acid suppression and listeriosis, incorporating the impact of reduced stomach acidity on bacterial growth and host immune response. The model reveals that gastric acid suppression can expedite listeriosis onset, and that a certain level of immune response is necessary to prevent infection. The findings suggest that gastric acid suppression can create conditions favorable for listeriosis, and that a certain level of immune response is necessary to prevent infection.

This research investigates the impact of hardware impairments on a secure multi-user communication system that utilizes reconfigurable intelligent surfaces and employs hybrid analog-and-digital beamforming. The study derives closed-form expressions for the achievable data rates of the system, considering different impairment scenarios. The results show that the impact of hardware impairment is more pronounced in scenarios with high signal strength, and that the system's performance is significantly affected by impairments such as phase noise and hardware impairments. The research also highlights the importance of optimizing beamforming vectors to mitigate the effects of hardware impairment.

This behavior is consistent with a model in which the soft light curve is delayed relative to the hard light curve due to the time it takes for the soft photons to escape from the accretion disk. Our analysis of the coherence and phase lag in Cygnus X-1 provides important constraints on the properties of the accretion disk and the dynamics of the system.

The precise modeling of CPA and NLO-based laser systems is a complex task.
A new, unified model has been developed to address this challenge, combining
ray-tracing and wavefront propagation techniques with a unified approach.
This model is versatile and can be applied to a wide range of laser systems,
including CPA, NLO, and MPO systems. It is capable of handling various types of
optical components and multiple propagation methods. The model's capabilities
are demonstrated through modeling a 100-Hz, 100-J laser system.

Multimodal text generation is a complex task that requires generated text to be both contextually coherent and image-relevant. Current methods often struggle to balance these requirements, as they tend to prioritize one aspect over the other. The proposed MAGIC framework addresses this challenge by employing a multi-objective approach that simultaneously optimizes text coherence and image relevance. The framework consists of two key components: a context-driven text generation model and a relevance-aware discriminator. The discriminator evaluates the relevance of generated text to the input image and guides the generator to produce text that is both coherent and image-relevant. The generator is further enhanced by incorporating a relevance loss term and a relevance discriminator network. The MAGIC framework was tested on the MS-COCO dataset and demonstrated superior performance in multiple text generation metrics, including BLEU, METEOR, and CIDEr.

A new Delegated RingCT signature scheme is proposed, building upon the existing RingCT model, to address its limitations in speed and scalability. The Delegated RingCT scheme employs a combination of the Chaum-Pedersen signature and the Verkle tree data structure to ensure transaction privacy while improving efficiency. The proposed scheme achieves a significant speedup, processing 100,000 signatures per second, and enhances scalability by reducing the size of the proof from 1.5 MB to 100 KB. The scheme's security is formally proven, relying on the discrete logarithm problem and the random oracle model.

The beam-beam interaction in the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) is a complex phenomenon that can be measured using the closed orbit shift and beam size increase. Recent studies have revealed that the beam-beam effect is more pronounced than anticipated, with significant implications for the performance of the LHC. To investigate this phenomenon, researchers have developed a method to directly measure the beam-beam effect by analyzing the closed orbit differences and beam sizes at the interaction points. This method has been successfully applied to the LHC, with results indicating that the beam-beam effect is more pronounced than previously thought. To further understand this phenomenon, researchers have proposed a new method to measure the beam-beam effect using the beam sizes and closed orbit differences. This method has been validated using simulations and has shown promising results.

Machine learning models for solid mechanics, particularly those simulating material behavior, are often developed using neural networks. However, these models typically require a substantial amount of data and are not easily adaptable to continual learning. This paper presents a groundbreaking approach to continual learning in the context of solid mechanics, utilizing a neural network-based constitutive model. The model is trained on data from uniaxial tensile tests and successfully captures the material's plasticity behavior, even in complex scenarios such as combined loading and cyclic tests. The proposed method involves developing a novel data augmentation technique and leveraging a physics-informed loss function to enhance the model's performance. The results demonstrate that this approach can significantly reduce the need for experimental data and enable the model to accurately predict material behavior under various complex conditions.

A recent study of the $\Xi(10753)$ resonance, conducted by the BESIII Collaboration, has generated significant interest in the particle physics community. Our analysis reveals that this resonance can be accommodated within the conventional bottomonium framework, specifically as a $1^{3}D_{1}$ state. Furthermore, we have determined the mass of the $\Xi(10753)$ to be $10753.2 \pm 1.0$ MeV, and our findings are consistent with predictions made by QCD sum rules.

SGD is a widely used optimization technique for training quantized neural networks, but training these models with AskewSGC is significantly more efficient. Our experiments demonstrate that AskewSGC outperforms conventional methods in training quantized neural networks, achieving better results in less time.

The growing interest in soft robotics has led to the development of robots with unique designs that differ significantly from the limb structures of animals. This is largely due to the limited use of joints in soft robots, which are often replaced by flexible joints. In contrast, this paper presents a novel soft robot inspired by the limb structure of invertebrates and vertebrates, utilizing multiple actuated segments. The proposed robot features a soft exoskeleton that enables the transmission of actuation to multiple flexible joints, allowing for a wide range of motion. The effectiveness of this design is demonstrated through the successful implementation of a walking gait, which showcases the robot's potential for complex movement.

This paper extends a previous study by providing explicit forms for left-invariant metrics on the Jacobi group in both real and complex forms, and relating them to Kähler metrics on the Siegel-Jacobi upper half-plane. Specifically, the paper establishes connections to Kähler balanced metrics and their extensions. Additionally, the paper derives expressions for the curvature tensor and curvature operator, and identifies conditions under which the Jacobi group admits a non-trivial derivation.

We introduce FactVerify, a fact verification dataset comprising 12,000 statements that require verification against information from multiple sources, including multiple Wikipedia articles. The dataset encompasses a range of verification tasks, including the analysis of complex statements that are broken down into multiple subclaims to enhance the performance of fact verification. The research also introduces a new verification model, which leverages the decomposed subclaims to improve the accuracy of the analysis. The dataset is available at https://github.com/robinmccann/factverify.

This study presents an innovative approach to developing generative models without relying on manually labeled data, addressing a significant limitation in current research. The proposed framework utilizes a self-supervised learning method that leverages data augmentation and a variational autoencoder to generate synthetic samples. The framework's effectiveness is demonstrated through experiments on the MNIST dataset, showcasing its ability to produce high-quality data and generate a wide range of handwritten digits. The study's findings indicate that this approach is a promising direction for further research in unsupervised generative modeling.

This research focuses on developing algorithms for computing shortest paths in weighted graphs that are resilient to failures. Specifically, we investigate the efficiency of fault-tolerant distance labels and their applications to dynamic shortest path problems. Our proposed algorithms for both decremental and dynamic scenarios achieve improved performance by a factor of log n, surpassing previous results. Additionally, we introduce novel algorithms for achieving efficient all-pairs and single-source shortest path computations.

A novel approach for automatic brain tissue segmentation in T1-weighted MRI images is developed, leveraging the power of Gaussian Processes to identify and model distinct tissue patterns. The method generates a comprehensive atlas of the brain, which is then used to segment individual patient MRIs into distinct tissue types. The proposed technique is evaluated on a large dataset of 1,000 MRIs from the ADNI project, yielding superior results compared to a leading open-source segmentation tool, 3D Slicer.

A one-dimensional Bose gas is subjected to a time-varying modulation and thermal fluctuations from its surrounding environment. The interplay between the modulation and environmental influence is examined through a theoretical model that incorporates a specific type of thermalization process. The model reveals that the thermalization process can either hinder or facilitate the formation of a Bose condensate, depending on its characteristics. The model also indicates that the thermal fluctuations can lead to the emergence of a new type of phase transition, which is not present in a closed system. The findings have implications for the development of new types of quantum simulators and the study of non-equilibrium quantum systems.

We demonstrate that in the context of $p$-harmonic functions, the property of being convex is a rigid characteristic, provided $p < (\frac{n}{n-1})^2$. This outcome is a consequence of a more comprehensive finding, which reveals that a function $u$ is $W^{1,p}$ convex if and only if it is a convex function and satisfies a specific inequality, namely $D^2u \geq 0$ in a distributional sense. This inequality holds for any function $u$ that is upper semi-continuous and bounded below.

The performance of quantum clocks based on two-level systems and their measurement techniques are analyzed in this research. A key aspect of these systems is the influence of photodetection, which can significantly impact the clock's stability and accuracy. A comprehensive model is developed to describe the dynamics of these systems and their measurement processes, taking into account the effects of photodetection. A specific type of photodetection, which is commonly used in experiments, is examined in detail and its implications for clock stability and accuracy are explored. A trade-off between the sensitivity of the photodetection and the accuracy of the clock is identified and it is shown that this trade-off can be optimized by adjusting the system's parameters. A specific type of photodetection, which is used in experiments with Ramsey-type clocks, is examined in detail and it is shown that this type of photodetection can significantly impact the clock's stability and accuracy. This study introduces a novel optimization problem, known as Heuristic Online Energy and Failure Sensitivity (HFES), which seeks to minimize energy consumption in a network while maintaining reliability. To address this challenge, a two-step solution is presented. Initially, a mathematical model is developed to identify the most energy-efficient and reliable network paths. Subsequently, a novel algorithm, referred to as HFES, is designed to dynamically select these paths in real-time. The proposed HFES algorithm outperforms existing methods by achieving a 10% reduction in energy consumption and a 10% increase in reliability.

This research focuses on enhancing image retrieval performance by addressing the loss function's bias towards a few dominant features. We break down the pair-wise loss gradient into distinct components, each contributing differently to the learning process. By analyzing these components, we identify a particular aspect that hinders optimal feature learning and impairs retrieval performance. To counteract this, we propose a novel loss function that filters out the detrimental component, thereby enhancing the retrieval system's performance. Experiments conducted on public datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, yielding notable improvements in image retrieval.

We investigate the inherent limitations of a particular class of quantum codes, specifically those derived from single tensor structures, in the context of erasure correction. Our findings reveal that any quantum code based on a uniform tensor must adhere to strict constraints, which necessitate that the underlying tensor's underlying graph possesses a specific type of symmetry, namely vertex transitivity. Furthermore, we demonstrate that if the tensor's underlying graph exhibits only two distinct distances between nodes, then its structure is equivalent to a known family of quantum codes, specifically the quantum Gabidulin codes.

The origin of magnetized radio filaments in the universe remains a mystery, 
despite their presence in various environments.  Three theories have been put forth 
to explain their formation:  the first suggests they are a result of a 
gravitational instability in a filamentary structure, the second proposes they 
are a byproduct of a shock wave, and the third suggests they are a byproduct of 
a turbulent process.  We have analyzed the morphology of these filaments in 
detail, using a combination of observational data and simulations.  Our results 
indicate that the filaments exhibit a range of characteristics, including 
irregular shapes and varying intensities.  We have also found that the 
distribution of these filaments is not uniform, with some areas showing a 
higher concentration than others.  Our findings suggest that the filaments are 
likely a byproduct of a complex process involving multiple factors, including 
gravity, shock waves, and turbulence.

This research introduces a leader-follower control approach to optimize the operation of a network with distributed energy resources. By designating a specific node as the leader, it can provide information to its neighboring nodes, facilitating coordinated control of distributed energy resources. This method allows for a hierarchical control structure, enabling the leader to dictate the overall system behavior. The authors formulate a multi-objective optimization problem to determine the optimal leader-follower network configuration, aiming to minimize the total cost of distributed energy resources. The problem is initially complex and non-convex, but the researchers reformulate it into a convex optimization problem, making it more tractable. The proposed solution is validated through simulations on a 14-bus network, demonstrating its effectiveness in achieving the desired objectives.

This research presents a new framework for addressing a complex multi-agent problem, where multiple arms are available to choose from and each arm's reward is determined by a combination of individual and shared factors. The study derives upper and lower bounds on regret for this problem, revealing that significant losses or delays in identifying the optimal arm's performance can severely limit the potential for achieving optimal outcomes. A specific algorithm is proposed to address this issue, leveraging a technique that involves selecting a subset of arms to evaluate, and the research demonstrates that this approach can lead to reduced regret. The study also provides a lower bound on regret for this problem, and the findings indicate that the proposed algorithm is near-optimal.

We introduce a novel, theory-driven framework for dialogue generation, grounded in
semantics and logic, to provide a structured approach to developing text-generation systems.
Our aim is to create a comprehensive framework that can be applied to various types of dialogue,
including both single-turn and multi-turn conversations, as well as tasks that require reasoning.
By providing a clear and formal specification of the underlying concepts, our framework enables
the development of highly capable text-generation models that can be applied to a wide range of
dialogue tasks.

Quantum chromodynamics, formulated in the 1960s and 1970s, has undergone significant research and exploration, particularly regarding strong-interaction matter. Advances in experimental facilities such as RHIC and the LHC have provided new insights into this field. Theoretical and computational developments, including lattice QCD, have also contributed to our understanding. The study of QCD has led to the discovery of novel forms of matter, exemplified by the study of quark-gluon plasma, a state of matter that existed shortly after the Big Bang and is now studied in the laboratory.

The variability of loads on offshore wind turbines is heavily influenced by random factors such as turbulence and irregular waves. To better understand the impact of this variability, we have developed a method to quantify the extent of random loading on turbines. This method uses a statistical measure called the coefficient of variation, which we have applied to both short-term and long-term load data. By analyzing the relationship between the variability of loads and their average magnitude, we have found that the extent of random loading on turbines is relatively consistent across different timeframes. This has significant implications for the design of turbines, as it suggests that the extent of random loading should be considered in both short-term and long-term load assessments.

This research aims to develop a comprehensive framework for analyzing Twitter data during disasters, encompassing sentiment analysis, topic identification, and information extraction. By leveraging machine learning and natural language processing techniques, we aim to track the public's evolving emotions and opinions throughout a disaster event. Additionally, we propose a method to extract and categorize relevant information from disaster-related tweets, such as location, time, and event type. Our framework is evaluated using a large-scale dataset of Hurricane Harvey tweets, demonstrating its effectiveness in accurately predicting sentiment and identifying key topics. Moreover, we showcase the practical applications of our framework in generating real-time reports and visualizations, ultimately providing valuable insights to support disaster response efforts.

This paper defines the R*-nilpotency degree D*G of a group G and investigates its connection to the property of G being a hypercentral nilpotent group. We also establish a correspondence between the value of D*G and the lower central series of G.

A novel method for inverting the dielectric function is developed to analyze
data from ultrafast experiments, where the Kramers-Kronig relations are applied
to a complex spectrum, which is decomposed into a series of Lorentzian peaks.
The traditional approach to dielectric function inversion is highly sensitive to
noise, which is a significant issue in ultrafast experiments. To overcome this,
a new method is proposed that utilizes a regularization technique to mitigate
noise issues. This new approach is tested using noisy data and demonstrates its
robustness. Additionally, a novel method is introduced to determine the
dielectric function from a complex spectrum obtained from a Kramers-Kronig
discontinuous dataset.

This study presents a probabilistic approach to tracking objects in video footage captured from a moving vehicle. A Joint Probabilistic Data Association (JPDA) tracker is used to identify and follow objects, and a Bayesian framework is applied to analyze tracking performance. The results are then used to develop a driving scenario analysis tool.

This study introduces interface CFT, a framework for exploring entanglement in systems with boundaries. The framework is applied to the reflected entropy and Markov gap in various scenarios. The reflected entropy in certain configurations exhibits universal behavior analogous to that of the Markov gap in one-dimensional critical systems. The Markov gap also displays distinct characteristics in systems with boundaries, including a dependence on boundary conditions and a connection to the boundary central charge. The reflected entropy and Markov gap in systems with boundaries are found to be influenced by the boundary CFT$_1$ sector, and the research also reveals the relationship between these quantities and the boundary conditions. The study further explores the relationship between the reflected entropy and Markov gap in systems with boundaries and the mutual information in boundary ICFT$_1$.

This study proposes an enhanced extreme learning machine (ELM) channel estimation technique for systems with limited cyclic prefix length and imperfect hardware. The ELM is trained using a cyclic prefix and is then utilized to estimate channels during the data transmission period. The ELM's parameters are optimized using the least squares method, and its performance surpasses that of conventional methods, particularly in scenarios with insufficient cyclic prefix length and hardware impairments. The ELM's parameters are initially set to random values, and their effectiveness is demonstrated through simulation results.

In quantum mechanics, measuring non-projective states is often seen as unnecessary, as it can be replaced with projective measurements yielding similar results. However, this equivalence holds true only under specific conditions, namely when the measurement operators are part of a complete set. This paper demonstrates that, for certain scenarios, a non-projective measurement can be simulated by a projective measurement, but only when the measurement operators are not part of a complete set. This implies that, for these specific cases, a non-projective measurement can be carried out without needing to know the system's initial state. This has significant implications for the field of quantum information, particularly in the context of quantum state engineering.

We establish the rigidity of abelian instantons within the G2 instanton moduli space, 
and derive a local Atiyah-Hitchin type estimate for connections of low energy. 
Our findings suggest a potential approach to studying the Gluing Lemma in the context of G2 and 
3-form harmonic theory.

The COVID-19 pandemic has accelerated the adoption of contact tracing technologies, which can be used to identify and isolate individuals exposed to infected individuals. However, there are concerns that these technologies may be exploited for unrelated purposes, such as tracking individuals' movements and locations, leading to a potential decline in personal privacy and civil liberties. This paper explores the risks associated with contact tracing technologies, including a case study of a proposed system that could be manipulated to track individuals' movements. It also discusses the challenges of implementing these technologies and proposes a framework for evaluating their potential impact on personal privacy and civil liberties.

Our research investigates the effects of decoherence on the entanglement of two interacting quantum systems, where decoherence is modeled as a specific type of interaction between these systems and their surrounding environment. By analyzing a comprehensive set of equations, we demonstrate that decoherence can be understood as a unique interaction that not only influences individual systems but also generates quantum entanglement between subsystems and their environment. This insight reveals that decoherence is a fundamental component of the broader framework of open quantum systems, rather than an external factor.

We suggest using high-level language features translated into another language to verify correctness, which can be applied to any language with a suitable translation. In this paper, we examine the effectiveness of translating non-deterministic choice and partial functions into a functional language based on continuation-passing style, and we demonstrate this approach through the development of a compiler for C that generates equivalent Haskell code.

Recent research has uncovered a previously unknown species, Iochroma gonzaloii, which was initially thought to be a member of the I. cordifolium complex. A closer examination of the species' morphology, genetics, and geographical distribution has led to the identification of its unique characteristics. A molecular phylogenetic analysis of the Iochroma genus has been conducted using the plastid gene ndhF, and the results indicate that I. gonzaloii is not closely related to I. cordifolium, but rather to I. macrophyllum. A comparison of the species' morphological traits and their distribution patterns has been made, and the implications of these findings for the Iochroma genus have been discussed.

This study expands the integral relationship linked to Ramanujan's well-known identity for the zeta function, by using the Hurwitz zeta function to derive a generalized version. We also establish an analogous integral connection for general periodic zeta functions.

Our research focuses on computing the fixed-point set of the equivariant elliptic cohomology under the influence of a specific torus, $T$, acting on an algebraic variety. This specific torus has a specific property where its action is not fully compatible with the complex structure of the torus, and we have found that the fixed-point set is equivalent to the ordinary cohomology of the variety. This equivalence is established through a novel approach that involves the use of a specific type of curve, known as a bi-elliptic curve, and we have also shown that this approach can be used to compute the equivariant elliptic cohomology under the influence of a specific type of group action.

Our goal is to utilize unsupervised learning to gain insights into geometric data structures, specifically leveraging the power of deep learning to identify patterns in complex geometric data. To achieve this, we developed a novel approach that combines a deep autoencoder with a hierarchical Delaunay triangulation structure, allowing us to train the model in an unsupervised manner. By doing so, we can extract meaningful representations from the data, which can then be used to address challenging geometric problems. To validate our approach, we conducted experiments on the minimum spanning tree problem, demonstrating that the model can effectively learn and generalize this problem from synthetic data.

This study examines the end-to-end encrypted messaging app Signal's PIN security by exploring the understanding and usage of PINs among its users. The research involved 100 participants who completed a series of tasks to assess their knowledge and usage of Signal's PIN system. The findings indicate that users have a limited understanding of Signal's PIN purpose, with many using short, easily guessable PINs. The results also show that users are more likely to use a PIN if they are aware of its purpose, but many still use a PIN that can be cracked within seconds. The study's implications suggest that Signal should improve its onboarding process to educate users about the importance of a strong PIN and provide better guidance on creating a secure PIN.

This study presents the development of novel quadrature rules, specifically tailored for solar energy calculations, which are heavily influenced by the solar energy distribution. Traditional quadrature rules, like Gauss quadrature, are not ideal for such applications due to their reliance on uniform distributions. We propose two types of quadrature rules: one optimized for solar energy density and another for uniform density, which can be used to correct the former. These rules are based on a mathematical framework that allows for the approximation of integrals with high accuracy. We demonstrate the effectiveness of these rules through various examples, including those related to photovoltaic cells and radiative heat transfer, where they outperform traditional rules in terms of computational efficiency and accuracy.

In optimization, accurately determining eigenvalues and gradients is crucial for developing efficient second-order methods. However, current methods for computing these values are often too slow to be practical. We introduce ViViT, a novel approach that uses neural networks to predict eigenvalues and gradients, thereby improving the speed of the process. By leveraging a directional derivative, ViViT achieves faster computation times, outperforming existing methods. Furthermore, ViViT's ability to compute eigenvalues and gradients in real-time enables the development of efficient second-order methods, such as a novel optimization algorithm called SVI.

This study investigates the presence of gender bias in word embeddings by examining its effects across multiple languages and contexts. We employed a metric to quantify gender bias in word embeddings and evaluated its magnitude in relation to the gendered nature of training data. Our analysis of 12 languages revealed a correlation between grammatical gender systems and gender bias in word embeddings. Furthermore, we examined the influence of gendered language on bias and found that languages with gendered language exhibit a higher level of gender bias. To mitigate gender bias, we developed a method to adjust word embeddings by removing grammatical gender information. Our results indicate that this approach effectively reduces gender bias while maintaining contextual information in word embeddings.

This paper examines the dynamics of actions of solvable groups on character spaces of their commutator subgroups, generalizing the dynamics on Teichm\"uller space and moduli space of flat bundles. Our analysis reveals that, in contrast to torus actions, the action of solvable groups on these spaces is ergodic and exhibits chaotic behavior, with a single orbit densely populating the character variety in many cases.

This paper presents a novel approach to estimating the pose of a rigid object from a single image. The method utilizes a pre-trained neural network to identify keypoints on the object and then employs a probabilistic optimization technique to determine the object's pose. By accounting for uncertainty in the keypoints, the proposed approach achieves a 10% improvement in pose estimation accuracy over a baseline method and a 20% reduction in estimation error compared to a fully deterministic optimization technique.

This research introduces an innovative approach to predicting travel times in urban transportation systems using a combination of gradient boosting decision trees and data on vehicle movements. By leveraging vehicle trajectory information, our method achieves high accuracy in travel time forecasting, outperforming a graph neural network-based solution in both predictive accuracy and computational efficiency. We tested our approach on data from the city of Chicago and found that our model can accurately estimate travel times for individual trips, as well as provide reliable estimates for entire road networks. Additionally, our method is highly scalable and can be easily adapted to other cities with minimal adjustments.

Causal inference techniques have been increasingly applied to machine learning, with growing interest in addressing sensitive issues such as bias and fairness. This paper focuses on counterfactual fairness, a concept that assesses whether a classification outcome would remain unchanged if sensitive variables were altered. To address this, we propose a novel approach that integrates causal reasoning into classification models, enabling the detection of causal relationships between features and targets, and the identification of relevant variables. This framework can be applied to both linear and non-linear models, with our experiments demonstrating its effectiveness in addressing fairness issues.

The upcoming generation of radio telescopes will be able to handle vast amounts of data generated by their instruments. To effectively manage this data, processing will need to occur locally, close to the data creation point. This will require a shift in how data is handled, with a greater emphasis on data analysis performed on the data itself rather than on file-based operations. To facilitate this, a new data management system is being developed, with a focus on providing a unified data analysis environment that can be accessed remotely. This paper outlines the design and implementation of this new system, with a specific emphasis on its ability to support data analysis performed on data streams.

This study proposes a novel approach to predicting a movie's anticipated earnings based on its cast's star power. Star power is determined through a supervised learning model that utilizes revenue data from movies featuring the respective actors. To address the issue of skewed revenue distribution, we employ a log-transformed target variable. Additionally, we develop a Bayesian network to model the relationships between actors in a movie, and we use this network to calculate a measure of diversity among the cast. Finally, we apply a linear regression model to analyze the relationship between star power, cast diversity, and a movie's revenue.

This paper presents a comprehensive stability analysis of power systems, incorporating the effects of secondary frequency control and economic dispatch on system stability. A novel approach is introduced to model the interaction between primary frequency control and economic dispatch, and its impact on system stability is investigated. A key finding is that secondary frequency control can significantly alter the location of the system's eigenvalues, and under certain conditions, it can enhance or degrade system stability. This research provides valuable insights for system operators to optimize economic dispatch settings, thereby improving power system stability.

This paper explores the concept of separation within the context of connected cyber-physical systems, focusing on the distinction between communication and computation layers. We examine the properties required to ensure secure interactions between these layers, considering the presence of potential intruders. Our analysis involves the development of novel separation models, which we demonstrate to be equivalent to established models in the literature. Furthermore, we apply our findings to a specific cyber-physical system, a smart home, to illustrate their practical implications.

The polarization of high-energy emissions from blazars can provide valuable insights into their surrounding astrophysical conditions. To study this, we conducted a multi-wavelength analysis of the flat-spectrum radio quasar PKS 0537-441, which exhibited strong gamma-ray emissions in 2015. By combining data from the Swift UV and X-ray telescopes, we found that the source's X-ray emissions were dominated by the relativistic jet, with a flat spectrum and a high degree of polarization. Our findings suggest that the jet's electrons were responsible for the observed gamma-ray emissions, with a high Lorentz factor of 10.5. Additionally, we found that the jet's magnetic field was aligned with the direction of the source's motion, with a high degree of polarization. Our results have important implications for the study of blazars and their surrounding environments.

The nature of replica-symmetry breaking in hessian landscapes is investigated, with a focus on how it differs between one-step and many-step structures. Our analysis reveals that one-step structures exhibit a single discontinuous eigenvalue shift, whereas many-step structures display a multi-step eigenvalue shift. Furthermore, we discovered that the nature of replica-symmetry breaking is determined by the distribution of overlap matrices' eigenvalues. Our research also highlights the importance of replica-symmetry breaking in understanding the nature of complex systems.

We've developed and tested various online methods for finding symmetric states with a fixed overlap, using an approach where we calculate the overlap between the true state and our estimate at each step. Our results show that these online schemes can't identify three states with a fixed overlap, but they can successfully identify two such states. We've also found that an online method can be as effective as a more complex offline approach in identifying two states with a fixed overlap.

A novel method for modeling light baryons in QCD is introduced, which utilizes the mass spectrum of light mesons to determine the light baryon masses. This approach is based on a lattice QCD calculation of the light baryon light-cone distribution amplitude, which is then used to derive the light baryon masses. The resulting mass spectrum is in good agreement with experimental data, and the method is found to be robust and insensitive to the chosen parameters. The model also provides a theoretical explanation for the light baryon mass spectrum, and the method is found to be applicable to a wide range of light baryons.

The sun's meridional circulation is a fundamental component of its internal dynamo, yet its characteristics are still not fully understood. Recent studies have suggested that the sun's meridional flow may be influenced by acoustic waves, but this has been difficult to verify due to the lack of observational evidence. This study aims to investigate the sun's meridional circulation by analyzing the sun's acoustic wave propagation times in the mid-latitudes. By examining the sun's acoustic wave propagation times, we found that the sun's meridional flow is present and exhibits a distinct pattern that is consistent with previous observations. This discovery provides a new method for studying the sun's meridional circulation and its potential impact on the sun's dynamo.

The presence of a primordial magnetic field can significantly impact gravitational waves, altering their propagation and potentially leading to observable effects such as polarization and speed variations. In this study, we examine the influence of a magnetic field on the generation and detection of gravitational waves, particularly focusing on the enhanced sensitivity of future detectors to these effects. Our findings suggest that detector arrays can effectively distinguish between different scenarios of primordial magnetic field strength, with even weak fields detectable by current and future instruments.

This paper presents a novel 4D light field image compression framework called
DC-LF. By utilizing the disparity information, the 4D light field images are
segmented into multiple planes, each representing a distinct epipolar line. A
single deep neural network is employed to compress these disparity-aware planes,
resulting in significantly improved compression efficiency. Experimental
results demonstrate the superiority of the proposed method over existing
solutions, with a rate-distortion gain of up to 1.5 dB and 16% in terms of
compression ratio.

This research addresses the challenge of cross-lingual information retrieval, where a query in one language must be matched with documents in a different language. The study presents a novel semi-interactive approach that leverages a pre-trained language model to predict lexical translations and then uses these predictions to calculate retrieval scores. The proposed method outperforms existing baselines on three datasets for both English-German and English-Russian language pairs. The source code and preprocessed datasets are available for reference.

This paper introduces a novel approach to tackle the issue of estimating demographic parameters from spatially distributed data with a high level of detail. The proposed method utilizes a spatially continuous model, which is then approximated using a finite element method to generate a Gaussian process. Demographic parameters are estimated by maximizing the likelihood function, which is derived from the Gaussian process. To address the issue of high dimensionality, which often arises in demographic models, the proposed method employs a variational inference technique to approximate the posterior distribution. The efficacy of the proposed approach is demonstrated through a simulated study, which involved the estimation of the diffusion coefficient and initial population density from population density data collected at a high level of detail.

This research introduces a quantum memory betting model where past outcomes influence the next event's probability. We examine the model's properties and provide an analytical solution for the optimal gambling strategy and long-term growth rate. Notably, the optimal strategy is state-dependent, and we find that the growth rate can be less than the optimal rate for certain memory lengths. We also explore the model's relationship to the free gambling system and identify a unique case where the optimal strategy remains constant.

ADCs are used in various fields, including astronomy, to measure light intensity across different wavelengths. To analyze data collected by ADCs, models are used to describe the relationship between wavelength and dispersion. This study examines the effects of atmospheric dispersion on ADC designs and data analysis, and compares the accuracy of different models. The results indicate that using the Cauchy model can lead to inaccuracies, particularly in the blue range, and that the Bessel model is more suitable for analyzing data collected by ADCs. The study also demonstrates that using the Bessel model can lead to more accurate results, and that the models can be used to estimate the atmospheric dispersion coefficient.

We've developed a Bayesian neural network model that incorporates a Horseshoe prior to tackle the challenge of modeling complex, non-linear relationships in high-dimensional data. This combination allows for the detection of non-linear relationships in the input variables and the identification of relevant variables. The model's effectiveness is demonstrated through its application to a simulated dataset and a real-world analysis of the 2016 US presidential election results.

In this paper, local type spaces in continuous logic are linked to the duality of abelian groups, leading to local Pontryagin duality, and further establishing connections between local type spaces and local Boolean algebras of closed sets, along with their topological relationships.

This paper presents a unified framework that integrates fairness, federated learning, and differential privacy to address privacy and ethical concerns in machine learning. The proposed framework incorporates metrics for evaluating fairness, privacy protection, and model performance, and uses these metrics to formulate optimization objectives. By leveraging these objectives, the framework enables the development of models that balance accuracy, fairness, and privacy in a unified manner. The framework is demonstrated through a numerical example, and its effectiveness is evaluated in terms of its impact on model performance and the trade-offs between privacy, fairness, and accuracy.

This study investigates the influence of a $Z'$ boson resonance on dark matter (DM) searches and its implications for experimental searches at the LHC. We examine the DM annihilation process that involves the exchange of both the $Z$ and $Z'$ bosons, which can significantly impact the DM relic abundance and its detection in direct searches. Furthermore, we explore how the DM's interaction with the $Z'$ boson affects its relic abundance and how this interaction can be exploited to enhance the DM's sensitivity to the $Z'$ boson at the LHC. We demonstrate that DM searches can be optimized by considering the interference between the $Z$ and $Z'$ bosons, thereby increasing the DM's sensitivity to the $Z'$ boson. We also investigate the DM's interaction with the $Z'$ boson and its implications for the DM's relic abundance and its detection in future experiments.

This paper presents a novel deep unsupervised learning method for tackling complex optimization issues in wireless communication systems. The proposed approach utilizes a variational autoencoder to tackle the challenging problem of assigning users to base stations in a high-load scenario. By leveraging this method, we can achieve a performance comparable to a meticulously designed genetic algorithm, albeit with a significant reduction in computational complexity. The results demonstrate that our deep learning-based solution can be up to 100 times faster than the genetic algorithm, making it an attractive option for real-time applications.

A theoretical model has been developed to describe the distribution of beta-strength in a nucleus, taking into account the unique characteristics of both the parent and daughter nuclei, as well as the individual properties of the decaying particles. By applying this model to a specific case of a neutron-rich tin isotope, we have been able to compare our results with recent experimental data obtained through a beta-delayed neutron resonance ionization detection technique. Our calculations reveal that the dominant component of the beta-strength in this nucleus is concentrated at lower energy levels, while the remaining strength is fragmented across a range of higher energies. Furthermore, we have found that the distribution of this higher-energy strength is influenced by the specific configuration of the decaying particles, with the highest-energy component being associated with a particular orbital.

We examine a model where dark matter is comprised of both vector and scalar particles, with the scalars being the sole mediators between the dark and visible sectors. The scalar sector is linked to right-handed neutrinos, which may be responsible for dark matter's relic density. The model's implications for right-handed neutrino masses and lepton flavor violation are also explored.

This paper presents an innovative learning-based control strategy that integrates a pre-trained reinforcement learning model with a carefully designed trajectory tracking algorithm. The proposed method is specifically tailored for systems with limited available data, where traditional reinforcement learning methods often fall short. To address this limitation, our approach leverages the knowledge gained from a pre-trained policy, which is trained using a large-scale dataset. The resulting controller is then fine-tuned to optimize performance on specific trajectory tracking tasks. The efficacy of this novel control strategy is demonstrated through a case study on a quadrotor system, where it is shown to outperform traditional reinforcement learning methods in terms of tracking accuracy and robustness.

The Ward identities associated with spin-three symmetry in the Toda conformal field theory are derived and their connection to higher-spin theory is demonstrated. Specifically, it is shown that the spin-three Ward identities can be obtained from a subset of higher-spin equations. Furthermore, the theory's correlation functions are linked to the correlation functions of higher-spin theory through a direct comparison.

We have developed a novel GAN architecture called relation network, which utilizes a fully-connected network to enhance the mapping between generated and real images. This approach surpasses previous methods, such as spectral normalization and self-enforcing GANs, in terms of generated image quality and training stability. Our results demonstrate that the relation network can be applied to various image generation tasks, including those involving different resolutions and styles, and can significantly enhance the performance of GANs in these scenarios.

Twin-field quantum key distribution (TF-QKD) has emerged as a leading approach for long-distance secure communication. Despite its potential, a major obstacle remains in synchronizing the phases of distant devices, which can be addressed by a novel method presented in this research. By incorporating a reference frame, our approach enables a shared global phase reference for TF-QKD systems. Furthermore, our method is versatile and can be applied to various TF-QKD implementations, including decoy-MZTF-QKD, phase-encoding TF-QKD, and its variants.

This paper examines the characteristics of Toeplitz operators within specific function spaces, namely the $p$-Bergman and $p$-Fock spaces. Our investigation centers on determining the space of symbols associated with these operators and establishing their continuity properties.

This paper presents a new, straightforward method for automatically creating
annotated data for object detection tasks.  Our technique utilizes a pre-trained
object detector to generate labels for images that are then manually marked with
key points.  These labels and key point annotations are used to train object
detectors that perform significantly better than traditional annotation methods.
To facilitate the use of this new annotation format, we developed an open-source
tool that streamlines the process of manually labeling data.  Our method is
demonstrated through experiments on the Pascal VOC dataset, where we show that
it can improve the performance of state-of-the-art object detectors.

The central molecular zone (CMZ) in the Milky Way's center is a key area for understanding the connection between star formation and gas. A key area within the CMZ, the Sgr B2 region, is heavily influenced by nearby stars. Observations of molecular gas in this region are complicated by the presence of ionized gas, which can be affected by self-absorption. A study using the ALMA telescope has found that ionized gas in the Sgr B2 region is influenced by nearby stars, which can be observed through a phenomenon called self-absorption.
